articles.interpretacion_ecg:
The ECG recording showed wide QRS-complex (50 milliseconds; upper reference limit,4 40 milliseconds) tachycardia at a rate of 240 beats/min (Figure 1). The P waves were monomorphic; positively deflected in leads I, II, III, and aVF; and maximally negatively deflected in lead aVR. The P-wave mean electrical axis was normal (60 degrees; sinus P-wave reference interval,4 0 to 90 degrees); therefore, it was determined that the sinus node was the most likely origin of atrial depolarization. The PR interval was constant and less than the lower reference limit (40 milliseconds; PQ interval reference range,4 50 to 90 milliseconds). The QRS complexes were inspected for evidence of ventricular pre-excitation; however, delta waves were not identified in any of the leads. There was a single atrial premature complex (APC) identified with a coupling interval of 300 beats/min. The P wave had a similar morphology to the sinus P waves, and the PR interval remained short.

A short and static PR interval without apparent ventricular pre-excitation could occur as a result of 1 of 2 possible conduction disturbances: a focal junctional tachycardia (JT) with isorhythmic atrioventricular dissociation (IAVD) and type II synchronization or an atriohisian accessory pathway. For this cat, a focal JT with IAVD was considered unlikely because the APC had the same P-QRS relationship as did the sinus rhythm. As such, these findings were most consistent with a diagnosis of sinus tachycardia with evidence of conduction across an atypical (atriohisian) accessory pathway. There was no evidence of a reciprocating tachycardia in the cat during hospitalization.

In addition to abnormal conduction from the atria to the ventricles, there was evidence of an intraventricular conduction disturbance. The widened QRS complexes were further characterized by the presence of a deep S wave that contributed to > 50% of the QRS width in the tracings from inferior leads II, III, and aVF (Figure 2). In lead aVR, the QRS complexes were splintered resulting in an R-R′ morphology. The net negative deflection of the QRS complexes in leads I and aVF indicated an axis deviation in the right superior direction (–120 degrees; QRS complex mean electrical axis reference interval,4 0 to 160 degrees). These findings together were consistent with an incomplete right bundle branch block (RBBB).5

The cat was treated with furosemide and pimobendan for congestive heart failure; clopidogrel was also administered for thromboprophylaxis. Given the marked left atrial enlargement and smoke detected echocardiographically, the cause of the neurologic episodes was suspected to be secondary to embolization of an intracardiac thrombus to the brain or spinal cord. At a recheck examination 1 week later, 6-lead ECG revealed a persistently shortened PR interval (40 milliseconds; PQ interval reference range,4 50 to 90 milliseconds) with sinus tachycardia at 240 beats/min. Resolution of congestive heart failure was evident on thoracic radiographs. There remained no evidence of ventricular pre-excitation or macroreentrant tachycardia. The neurology service was consulted, and a neurologic examination revealed C1-C5 myelopathy suggestive of a vascular event or less likely a neoplastic, infectious, or inflammatory process.

articles.discusion:
Discussion

An accessory pathway refers to a conducting fiber that connects 2 regions of electrically excitable cardiac tissue outside of normal atrioventricular (AV) nodal-His-Purkinje conduction system.6 The most commonly reported type of accessory pathway in humans and in veterinary species are AV accessory pathways. This type of pathway acts as a direct connection between the atria and the ventricles, and may allow for anterograde (AV), retrograde (ventriculoatrial), or bidirectional conduction. The direction of electrical conduction across an accessory pathway predisposes to the propagation of orthodromic or antidromic AV reciprocating tachycardias. A diagnosis of Wolf-Parkinson-White syndrome is made for patients that have clinical signs secondary to an AV reciprocating tachycardia. An AV accessory pathway may be identified by the presence of ventricular pre-excitation during sinus rhythm. This phenomenon occurs when there is antegrade conduction along an AV accessory pathway as well as normal conduction through the AV nodal-His-Purkinje system.6 This results in a fusion of these 2 waves of depolarization in the ventricular myocardium. Ventricular pre-excitation is identified on ECG as widening of the QRS complex due to the presence of a delta wave and the presence of a shortened PR interval. A delta wave is an alteration of the initial portion of the QRS complex because of slow conduction through the ventricular myocardium immediately adjacent to the AV accessory pathway. A shortened PR interval occurs because the wave of depolarization does not slow as it passes through the AV accessory pathway; this results in early depolarization of the adjacent ventricular myocardium.6,7

Other types of accessory pathways, collectively known as variant accessory pathways, have been identified in people and may involve anatomic substrates that are not limited to the ventricular and atrial myocardium.6 Examples of variant accessory pathways include atriohisian, nodoventricular, and fasciculoventricular. Atriohisian accessory pathways originate from the proximal portion of the AV junction (known as the proximal AV bundle) and terminate at the bundle of His, ultimately bypassing the compact AV node and producing a narrow QRS complex without a delta wave on ECG recordings.6,7 The PR interval, however, is short because the conduction velocity does not slow down as it passes through the atriohisian accessory pathway. The existence of these intranodal or paranodal bypass tracts is controversial; however, histopathological evidence for those bypass tracts has been found in human patients.8,9 In the cat of the present report, an atriohisian accessory pathway was the most likely explanation of the ECG findings. This variant accessory pathway has not previously been described in cats, to our knowledge.

An alternative explanation for the cat’s ECG findings was JT with IAVD. This condition is composed of 2 linked rhythms: an underlying sinus rhythm that produces the P waves and an accelerated junctional rhythm that produces the QRS complexes. The tandem rhythms discharge at similar rates and express type I or type II synchronization secondary to multifactorial physiologic properties (ie, response to arterial baroreceptors or pulsation of the sinus node artery). Type I synchronization refers to a continuous fluctuation in the P-QRS relationship, whereas type II synchronization refers to a consistent P-QRS relationship. In the cat of the present report, the rhythm aligned with JT with IAVD and type II synchronization.10 However, this rhythm was considered unlikely in this case, because there was a preserved P-QRS relationship during an APC (Figure 1). The presence of an APC during JT with IAVD and type II synchronization would result in a relatively longer P′R interval. The mean electrical axis of the P′ wave indicated that the atrial ectopic impulse originated from the lateral and superior portion of the right atrium; as such, it was expected to pass through the atrial myocardium and into the AV nodal-His-Purkinje system resulting in a normal P′R interval.

The wide QRS-complex morphology in the case described in the present report was the result of S-wave prolongation rather than ventricular pre-excitation. A deep S wave in the inferior leads (ie, leads II, III, and avF), QRS splintering in lead aVR resulting in a R-R′ morphology, and the right axis deviation were findings consistent with an incomplete RBBB. The modest increase in QRS-complex duration (50 milliseconds) aligned with incomplete RBBB. In cats, RBBB with a QRS-complex duration > 60 milliseconds was consistent with complete RBBB.5 This intraventricular conduction disturbance was likely secondary to the cat’s underlying cardiomyopathy. An alternative explanation for these ECG findings was severe right ventricular hypertrophy, because an incomplete RBBB morphology can exist without true damage to the right bundle branch.5 Echocardiography did not identify right ventricular hypertrophy; therefore, right ventricular hypertrophy was unlikely to have contributed to the incomplete RBBB pattern in this case.

Atriohisian tracts were previously implicated in humans who had short PR intervals and narrow QRS complexes without delta waves on ECG. Some people with atriohisian accessory pathways develop paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardias, resulting in the clinical syndrome known as Lown-Ganong-Levine syndrome.11 Currently, evidence that these accessory pathways serve as anterograde or retrograde limbs in supraventricular tachycardias remains to be established.6,7 There seems to be a low potential for development of a reciprocating tachycardia along an atriohisian accessory pathway, although the clinical relevance and prognosis for variant accessory pathways in cats are unknown. For the cat of the present report, there was no evidence of reciprocating tachycardia on initial and recheck ECG recordings. The cat’s history and physical examination and echocardiographic findings were most supportive of a thromboembolic event within the CNS. Intermittent tachyarrhythmias could not be completely ruled out but were not highly likely in this case.

Figure 1
Lead I, II, and III ECG traces obtained from a 7-year-old domestic shorthair cat following a sudden onset of incoordination. There is a sinus tachycardia with a heart rate of 240 beats/min. The PR interval is short (duration, 40 milliseconds), and the QRS complex is wide (duration, 50 milliseconds). There is no evidence of a delta wave in the initial portion of the QRS complexes; instead, the QRS complexes are wide as a consequence of an incomplete right bundle branch block. articles.interpretacion_ecg: The ECG tracing revealed an underlying sinus rhythm. Narrow QRS complexes were followed by a single wide QRS complex with a consistent PR interval and deep S wave in leads II, III, and aVF, consistent with a right bundle branch block (RBBB).1 An initial wide QRS complex is followed by a blocked P wave, suggestive of 2° AV block, and then subsequent, successive wide QRS complexes were followed by a blocked P wave, again consistent with 2° AV block. Prior to each blocked P wave, there was a constant PR interval, as with Mobitz type II 2° AV block. The development of transient RBBB in association with a change in ventricular rate produced by the 2° AV block was consistent with aberrant conduction. The diagnosis was sinus rhythm with Mobitz type II 2° AV block with linking phenomenon.

articles.discusion:
Discussion

Aberrant conduction is a ventricular conduction phenomenon defined as a transient block of the ventricular conduction system. This differs from a bundle branch block, which is an anatomic (fixed) block. Aberrant conduction occurs when an impulse reaches the conduction system before the interventricular conduction system has had time to completely repolarize.1 The duration of a refractory period changes with cycle length; the refractory period is shortened when there is an increase in heart rate and is prolonged when there is a decrease in heart rate. There are 2 forms of aberrant conduction, namely tachycardia-dependent (phase 3 aberrancy) and bradycardia-dependent (phase 4 aberrancy) blocks.2

A form of phase 3 aberrancy, Ashman phenomenon, was first described by Gouaux et al3 in association with atrial fibrillation. The generation of this aberrancy is dependent on the duration of the preceding cycle. A longer cycle preceding a shorter cycle can cause the right bundle branch to become refractory.3 If the conduction of the next impulse after a shorter R-R interval occurs, the right bundle branch will become refractory.3 The resulting aberrant conduction is termed Ashman phenomenon. For the cat of the present report, because the RBBB occurred when the cycle duration decreased and the heart rate accelerated, tachycardia-dependent RBBB with phase 3 aberrancy was initially considered; however, this would not explain the second aberrantly conducted QRS complex.

The underlying mechanism of the transient but sustained nature of the tachycardia-induced aberrant conduction in the cat of the present report can be explained by the linking phenomenon. The linking phenomenon requires a macroreentrant circuit where there are 2 branches with different properties.3–5 There is a dominant and a dependent pathway, which in this cat were the left bundle branch and right bundle branch, with preferential conduction through the dominant pathway and a dependent pathway that is characterized by a longer refractory period.2 An impulse can travel down the dominant pathway but is blocked in the dependent pathway; however, it can retrogradely travel back up the dependent pathway, resulting in prolonging the right bundle branch refractory state.2 The next antegrade impulse is not able to travel down the dependent pathway but conducts through the dominant branch and then reenters retrogradely.4,5 This will occur alternately until a change in cycle duration occurs and allows for full recovery of the pathways, thus resulting in a transient and nonsustained aberrancy.4

For the cat of the present report, the other ECG abnormality was Mobitz type II 2° AV block. Second-degree AV block in cats has been associated with cardiac disease and systemic illness, such as hyperthyroidism.6–8 Given that this cat had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, that condition may have been an underlying contributing cause of the 2° AV block.

articles.descripcion_del_caso:
A14-year-old 7.3-kg (16.1-lb) spayed female West Highland White Terrier was evaluated at a veterinary medical teaching hospital for possible pacemaker implantation to treat suspected sick sinus syndrome (SSS). Three days earlier, the dog had multiple collapse episodes; periods of sinus arrest were detected during an ECG examination. At that time, results of a CBC and serum biochemical analysis were within reference intervals. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mild myxomatous mitral and tricuspid valve degeneration without cardiac chamber enlargement (American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine classification1 stage B1) as well as mild pulmonary hypertension. The dog's history included chronic cough (presumed breed-related pulmonary fibrosis) for which theophylline (unknown dosage) was prescribed. After a diagnosis of SSS was made, theophylline administration was discontinued and terbutaline sulfate was prescribed at a dosage of 0.34 mg/kg (0.15 mg/lb) orally every 12 hours. Despite terbutaline administration, the dog continued to have syncopal episodes and was referred for possible pacemaker implantation.

On physical examination at the veterinary medical teaching hospital, findings included dull mentation, a grade II/VI left apical systolic murmur, bradycardia (heart rate, 36 beats/min) with an irregular cardiac rhythm. Three-view thoracic radiographic findings included mild generalized cardiomegaly and a mild diffuse interstitial pulmonary pattern, which were considered likely age-related changes; there was no evidence of cardiac decompensation or clear suspicion of pulmonary fibrosis. A serum electrolyte panel revealed hyperlactatemia (7.6 mmol/L; reference interval, 0 to 2.5 mmol/L) with no other notable electrolyte disturbances. Six-lead ECG and an atropine response test were performed.
articles.interpretacion_ecg:
The ECG recording at time of the evaluation revealed a highly irregular rhythm with a heart rate ranging from 20 to 200 beats/min (Figure 1). The rhythm had short periods of sinus tachycardia and frequent periods of sinus arrest lasting up to 6.5 seconds, followed by resumption of sinus tachycardia or occurrence of junctional escape complexes. The narrow, upright complex that terminated a prolonged sinus arrest was consistent with a junctional escape complex given its upright and narrow morphology, its occurrence following a pause, and the lack of a preceding P wave of sinus origin. The R-R interval immediately preceding the junctional escape complex measured 6,500 milliseconds, which is equivalent to an instantaneous rate of 9 depolarizations/min. This constellation of ECG findings (ie, short periods of sinus tachycardia, frequent periods of sinus arrest, and failure of the subsidiary pacemakers) when coupled with syncope is consistent with a diagnosis of SSS.2

The dog underwent an atropine response test in which an ECG examination was performed 30 minutes after SC administration of atropine sulfate at a dose of 0.04 mg/kg (0.018 mg/lb). After atropine administration, the ECG examination revealed sinus tachycardia at a rate of 220 beats/min with resolution of sinus arrest. This was considered a positive response to atropine administration; thus, medical management with propantheline bromide (4.3 mg/kg [1.95 mg/lb], PO, q 8 h) was initiated in addition to continued treatment with terbutaline.

The dog underwent continuous ECG monitoring in the intensive care unit. A 6-lead ECG examination was repeated the following day (Figure 2). This recording revealed a regular rhythm at a rate of 125 beats/min. Atrial depolarization (P') waves were seen as negative deflections in leads II, III, and aVF. The P’ waves were positive in all other evaluated leads. The duration of the PR interval (approx 60 milliseconds) was consistent and considered normal. The morphology of the QRS complexes was normal (upright and narrow), and each complex was associated with a P’ wave. Negative P’ waves can be observed when the atrial impulse originates in the lower (inferior) portions of the atria. Alternatively, negatively deflected P’ waves could represent retrograde conduction of P’ waves from a junctional rhythm or the combination of a junctional rhythm with type II isorhythmic atrioventricular dissociation. For the dog of the present report, the P’ waves were consistently associated with QRS complexes and had fixed, normal PR intervals; therefore, the possibility of a junctional rhythm with retrograde P’ wave conduction or with type II isorhythmic AV dissociation was considered less likely. The ECG findings were interpreted as consistent with a supraventricular rhythm with P’ waves that originated from the lower (inferior) portions of the atria and were responsible for generation of the associated QRS complexes. On the basis of the characteristic negative deflection of the P’ waves in leads II, III, and aVF, differential diagnoses for the origin of the atrial depolarizations included the coronary sinus (CS) or the inferior portion of the left atrium. Dextrocardia was another consideration but was ruled out by echocardiographic and thoracic radiographic findings, making coronary sinus rhythm (CSR) the probable diagnosis.

articles.discusion:
Discussion

Coronary sinus rhythm is proposed to be secondary to the presence of pacemaker cells in the region of the upper portion of the atrioventricular node extending into the CS.3 Anatomically, the CS courses along the sulcus between the left atrium and the left ventricle, and its ostium empties into the right atrium. The CS is the largest cardiac vein that receives blood from the coronary veins, and it extends from the valve of the great cardiac vein to the ostium of the CS.4

Embryologically, the CS is a left atrial structure.3,5 In humans, a small bundle of muscle fibers has been identified entering the atrioventricular node from the area of the CS.3,6 These muscle fibers are considered remnants of the left-sided sinoatrial (SA) node and have a structure similar to those in the SA node and the auricular musculature.3,6,7 Additionally, the CS region is notable for its abundance of ganglion cells.6 Therefore, the CS area likely possesses a high level of automaticity and possible pacemaker activity.3,6 The large number of ganglion cells renders this region quite sensitive to autonomic impulses.6

The ECG criteria for diagnosis of CSR include inverted (negative) P’ waves in leads II, III, and aVF; upright (positive) P’ waves in lead aVR; and P'R intervals of normal or slightly reduced duration in all recorded leads.3,5-9 All of these ECG findings were identified in the case described in the present report. Although not evaluated in this dog, an inverted (negative) P’ wave in lead V6 may also be observed with CSR.5 The generation of negatively deflected P’ waves in lead II is illustrated (Figure 3). Because the CS ostium is located in the posteroseptal region of the right atrium, impulses generated in this region would create a wave front in the opposite direction to the ones associated with impulses generated from the SA node.

In humans, CSR can be experimentally reproduced by use of a pacing catheter to stimulate an impulse in the orifice of the CS.3,5,8 Lau et al5 also found that these P'-wave changes are consistently observed in both dogs and humans when the os of the CS is electrically stimulated. Interestingly, these ECG criteria are achieved even when various regions of the great cardiac vein of dogs are electrically stimulated.5 In the experiment by Lau et al,5 pacing of the inferior left atrium in close proximity to the CS produced P’ waves identical to and indistinguishable from those observed with CSR. This indicates that the negatively deflected P’ waves of the dog of this report could also have originated from the inferior left atrium or along the great cardiac vein. The reason for this resemblance may be attributed to the common site of impulse formation or a common intra-atrial conduction pathway.5

Coronary sinus rhythm is believed to result from depression of pacemaker activity of the SA node.3 Experiments by Chiba and Hashimoto3 revealed that CSR could be induced by catecholamine injection into the CS region when the SA node activity is simultaneously suppressed by bethanechol injected into the sinus node artery in dogs. Therefore, CSR may develop when SA pacemaker activity is strongly suppressed, especially by cholinergic mechanisms, and when the CS region is stimulated by an adrenergic mechanism. To our knowledge, naturally occurring CSR in dogs has not been reported. The dog of the present report had SSS with depressed SA node activity. In addition, this dog had decreased vagal stimulation and increased sympathetic stimulation as a result of oral administration of propantheline and terbutaline, respectively. Although not identical, the condition of the dog of the present report was similar to that of the dogs with experimentally induced CSR in the study by Chiba and Hashimoto.3 However, in the case described in the present report, rhythms originating from the inferior left atrium could not be ruled out, and an intracardiac electrophysiologic assessment would be required for a definitive diagnosis.

articles.interpretacion_ecg: The ECG recording revealed an irregularly irregular rhythm with a calculated mean heart rate of 167 beats/min. There were positive deflections in the inferior leads corresponding to atrial depolarizations, with an atrial heart rate of 428 beats/min. Given the isoelectric line between the atrial waves, these deflections were consistent with the undulating appearance of flutter waves (F waves) suggestive of atypical atrial flutter (AFL). The F waves had variable morphologies and variable F-F intervals. The atrioventricular conduction ratio varied from 2:1 to 4:1, indicating variable second-degree atrioventricular block. Some of the QRS complexes were wide (duration, > 0.1 seconds) with positive deflections in leads II, III, and aVF, suggesting a left bundle branch block morphology. These wide and tall aberrant QRS complexes always followed a short R-R interval and were preceded by a relatively prolonged R-R interval. Therefore, the complexes were consistent with the Ashman phenomenon, the Brody effect, or aberrancy. The final ECG assessment was suspected macroreentrant supraventricular tachycardia, specifically atypical AFL. Additional electrophysiological studies would have been required to achieve a definitive diagnosis. Given the dog’s history of primary airway disease and absence of structural heart disease, the authors suspected that the AFL was related to the dog’s airway disease.

articles.discusion:
Discussion

Electrical reentry circuits can happen when anatomic or functional blocks and slow conduction areas are present together, along with electrical stimulation. Atrial fibrillation can be classified as a focal microreentrant mechanism; AFL can be classified as a macroreentrant mechanism.1 The pathophysiology of AFL is not fully understood. In people, researchers have shown that chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and obstructive sleep apnea are associated with increased risks of AFL, atrial fibrillation, or both.2,3 Patients with COPD who have more symptoms of respiratory distress have a higher risk of developing AFL or atrial fibrillation, and treating these patients with β-adrenoceptor blockers or surgical ablation can decrease the overall mortality rate,4 which makes diagnosing and treating AFL essential. However, no anti-arrhythmia medication was prescribed for the dog described in the present report at the time of evaluation.

In humans, COPD is defined as the presence of airflow limitation associated with an abnormal inflammatory response,5 and similar clinical signs of respiratory distress are observed in a variety of other species. In the dog described in the present report, respiratory distress secondary to pneumonia, pectus excavatum, and brachycephalic airway syndrome, with congenital abnormalities causing airway obstruction, was documented.6 Similar signs are observed in equine patients with recurrent airway obstruction caused by mucus obstructing the bronchioles and alveoli, defined as equine COPD.7

Studies8,9 have shown the close relationship between atrial fibrillation and chronic oxidative damage, acidosis, and systemic inflammation caused by COPD in people. A recent population-based cohort study8 reported that patients with COPD have greater systemic inflammation, as evidenced by higher plasma concentrations of inflammatory mediators such as high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-α, which correlated with a higher risk of developing AFL. Similarly, concentrations of tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-10, interleukin-13, and interleukin-17A were significantly higher in dogs with brachycephalic airway syndrome than in healthy dogs, but C-reactive protein, interleukin-1β, and interleukin-6 concentrations did not differ between these groups.6 Among these inflammatory mediators, tumor necrosis factor-α and its associated inflammatory pathways is one of the best characterized, and it has been shown that tumor necrosis factor-α is involved in atrial remodeling, including structural, electrical, and contractility changes, which are all contributing factors to the initiation and maintenance of atrial fibrillation.10 Moreover, high tumor necrosis factor-α concentrations can lead to atrial fibrosis in mice without causing significant changes in cardiac size or function while being arrhythmogenic.11 Fibrosis predisposes to the development of reentrant circuits by promoting conduction block and slow, heterogeneous conduction.12 The conduction abnormalities, in turn, play an important role in creating a unidirectional conduction block, which is necessary for development of atrial fibrillation.13 A transitional atrial fibrillation rhythm may also create a functional line of block and can be followed by stable AFL.14 In addition, an epidemiologic study15 found that a high percentage (47.8%) of brachycephalic dogs have high cardiac troponin I concentrations. Concurrent myocardial damage might contribute to the spontaneous development of AFL.

Medical treatment of AFL secondary to brachycephalic airway syndrome involves controlling the underlying inflammation. Evidence has shown that using low-dose methylprednisolone as a treatment significantly decreases the risk of redeveloping atrial fibrillation in people.16 Similarly, prednisone has been shown to prevent inducible AFL in dogs with experimentally induced sterile pericarditis.17 However, another study18 reported controversial results that NSAIDs other than aspirin could lead to a higher risk of AFL or atrial fibrillation. Owing to the similar pathophysiology and response to treatment between AFL and atrial fibrillation, it might be safe to hypothesize that AFL is also associated with high systemic inflammation caused by COPD. Although the exact cause of AFL still needs further investigation, to the authors’ knowledge, this is the first reported case that documented a potential relationship between brachycephalic airway syndrome in dogs and atypical AFL. However, other causes, such as Marfan syndrome and pectus excavatum, related to atrial fibrillation have also been reported in people.19,20

In conclusion, brachycephalic airway syndrome, which resembles COPD in people, may have led to the suspected atypical AFL in the patient of this report.

articles.descripcion_del_caso:
A 10-year-old 35-kg (77-lb) castrated male Golden Retriever was evaluated by the emergency service of a veterinary medical teaching hospital because of acute right hind limb lameness. On initial physical examination, the dog was overconditioned (body condition score, 7/9) with apparently normal mentation. Its rectal temperature was 39.6°C (103.3°F), mucous membranes were pink, and capillary refill time was < 2 seconds. During auscultation, the dog's heart rate was 100 beats/min and a regular rhythm was evident; a grade 4/6 systolic murmur with point of maximal intensity over the right apex was auscultated. Lung sounds were clear, with no detectible crackles or wheezes. Femoral pulses were strong and synchronous with the heartbeat. Radiography of the right hind limb revealed caudoventral luxation of the hip joint. The dog was hospitalized and administered a constant rate infusion of fentanyl (2 to 5 μg/kg/min [0.9 to 2.3 μg/lb/min) for pain management until surgical reduction of the hip joint luxation could be performed the next day.

Prior to anesthesia, a cardiology consultation was undertaken. During auscultation, the heart rate was 140 beats/min, and an irregular rhythm was noted with strong pulses and occasional pulse deficits. A grade 2 to 3/6 systolic left apical heart murmur and grade 2/6 systolic right apical murmur were detected. Thoracic radiography revealed moderate enlargement of the cardiac silhouette (vertebral heart score, 11.5; reference interval,1 9.2 to 10.2). The pulmonary veins were distended, and a mild bronchiolar pulmonary pattern was identified. Echocardiography revealed moderate to severe left atrial dilation (left atrial-to-aortic root diameter ratio, 2.04; reference interval,2 < 1.5), severe eccentric left ventricular hypertrophy (left ventricular internal dimension at end-diastole [normalized to body weight], 2.779; reference interval,2 < 1.8), and severe systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction, 25%; reference interval,2 45% to 65%), consistent with dilated cardiomyopathy. Six-lead ECG was performed.
articles.interpretacion_ecg:
Six-lead ECG performed during the cardiology consultation revealed a sinus rhythm with a heart rate of 120 beats/min as well as occasional single atrial premature complexes and occasional single, uniform ventricular premature complexes (Figure 1). The lead II tracing was used for analysis. The R-wave amplitude was high (4.9 mV; upper reference limit,3 3.0 mV), and the QRS-complex duration was prolonged (0.09 seconds; upper reference limit,3 0.07 seconds). The ST segment was 0.5 mV (upper reference limit, < 0.2 mV)3 less than the TP segment. The mean electrical axis was considered normal at +68°(reference interval, +40 to +100°).3 The measurement abnormalities indicated that there was a complete left bundle branch block and ST-segment depression. The presence of Q waves in the lead II tracing indicated that there was normal septal activation, which can occur with postdivisional complete left bundle branch block. The dog was deemed a suitable candidate for anesthesia, and screening for secondary causes of dilated cardiomyopathy was recommended. Administration of pimobendan was started at this time (0.35 mg/kg [0.16 mg/lb], PO, q 12 h).

Later that same day, a heart rate of 300 beats/min was auscultated immediately prior to anesthesia. The ECG recording at that time revealed an irregular rhythm, and the ventricular rate ranged from 280 to 300 beats/min (Figure 2). P waves were absent, and fibrillation waves (f waves) were observed as fine undulations along the baseline tracing. The QRS-complex duration was 0.08 seconds, the R-wave amplitude in the lead II tracing was 6.4 mV, and the mean electrical axis was +72°, similar to the previous ECG findings. ST-segment depression was suspected; however, the J point was less clearly defined, and this made measuring the ST segment more challenging. The ECG diagnosis was atrial fibrillation (AF) with a rapid ventricular response rate and a complete postdivisional left bundle branch block. The dog was administered a bolus of lidocaine hydrochloride (2 mg/kg [0.91 mg/lb], IV), which resulted in restoration of sinus rhythm with a heart rate of 83 beats/min (Figure 3). The dog was started on a constant rate infusion of lidocaine (60 μg/kg/min [27.3 μg/lb/min]).

The dog was anesthetized, and closed reduction of the right hip joint luxation was performed. Continuous telemetric ECG monitoring of the dog was performed in the hospital, starting at the time when AF was identified and continuing until the dog's discharge from the hospital. Single atrial premature complexes, single ventricular premature complexes, and short paroxysms of supraventricular tachycardia were noted overnight. There was no recurrence of persistent AF. Prior to the dog's discharge from the hospital, sinus rhythm with complete postdivisional left bundle branch block and ST-segment depression, similar to findings of the initial assessment, were identified in an ECG recording. Treatment with lidocaine was discontinued, and a tapering dose of amiodarone was started (11.4 mg/kg [5.2 mg/lb], PO, q 12 h for 7 days; 5.7 mg/kg [2.6 mg/lb], PO, q 12 h for 7 days; and then 5.7 mg/kg, PO, q 24 h until the owner was otherwise instructed).

articles.discusion:
Discussion

Atrial fibrillation is a supraventricular rhythm characterized on ECG recordings by narrow QRS complexes, an absence of P waves, irregular coupling intervals, and high ventricular response rates.4 Dogs with AF often have greater-than-normal atrial size owing to underlying structural heart disease; however, there is a subset of large-breed dogs that have AF with no discernable heart disease.5,6 Changes in autonomic tone have an important role in the initiation and perpetuation of AF.7–9 In the case described in the present report, AF was most likely a consequence of atrial fibrosis and dilation as well as decreased sympathetic tone and enhanced vagal tone secondary to fentanyl administration.

Atrial fibrillation may develop as a result of different mechanisms, including anatomic and functional reentry as well as rapidly discharging ectopic foci that commonly originate from the pulmonary veins.4,7–9 Reentry is a phenomenon that occurs when an area of myocardium that is initially refractory to electrical activity serves as a pathway to propagate electrical activity that re-excites the heart after the end of the refractory period.4,7–10 Factors that promote perpetuation of a reentry mechanism include atrial fibrosis, atrial stretch, short atrial refractory period, and dispersion of myocardial refractoriness.4,7–10 These factors help to create the necessary components of reentry, namely unidirectional block, slow conduction velocity, and appropriate cycle lengths.4,7–9 Atrial fibrosis is the most important determinant of AF in dogs with heart failure because it promotes reentry by physical separation of adjacent atrial muscle fibers; differentiation of fibroblasts into myofibroblasts, which interact with cardiomyocytes and promote arrhythmogenesis by causing slowing of conduction and spontaneous depolarization; and secretion of biologically active substances that have a paracrine effect on cardiomyocytes, thereby directly affecting their bioelectrical activity.8,9,11 Atrial dilation also promotes AF by achieving the critical mass needed to maintain a multiple circuit reentry mechanism and by increasing myocardial stretch, which promotes fibrillation.9 In the dog of the present report, moderate to severe left atrial enlargement was identified at the time of the first cardiology evaluation, indicating that the dog had the substrate for AF prior to the onset of the arrhythmia.

Changes in both parasympathetic and sympathetic tones can contribute to the development and maintenance of AF.5–8 Opioids alter synaptic neurotransmission to cardiac vagal nerves through the inhibition of presynaptic release of -aminobutyric acid that results in increased vagal tone.12 μ-Opioid receptor agonists also suppress the stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglia, which supplies sympathetic innervation to the heart, thereby promoting vagal tone dominance.13 The refractory period of the atrial tissues is shortened with increased vagal tone, which leads to a reduced wavelength that, in turn, promotes reentry. Wavelength is the dimension of the reentry circuit, and it is a product of conduction velocity and the refractory period. In addition, the heterogeneous distribution of parasympathetic innervation of the atria contributes to the variable repolarization. This increases the likelihood that recently excited cells will be near to cells that are recovering their excitability and will be available for reactivation. Therefore, it is suggested that the combination of vagally mediated shortening of the atrial action potential duration and an increase in the heterogeneity of refractoriness promotes reentry, leading to perpetuation of AF.7,8 Atrial fibrillation has been shown to occur spontaneously in anesthetized dogs receiving fentanyl as a consequence of enhanced vagal tone.14 As such, it was hypothesized that fentanyl contributed to the development and maintenance of AF in the dog of the present report.

Therapeutic management of AF is focused on controlling the ventricular response rate (rate control) or restoring and maintaining sinus rhythm (rhythm control). Rate control can be achieved with administration of negative chronotropic agents (eg, β-adrenoceptor agonists, select calcium channel blockers, and digoxin). Rhythm control has been achieved with administration of class I antiarrhythmic drugs, direct current electrical cardioversion, or both. Treatment with amiodarone has been shown to achieve rate or rhythm control.15 Regarding long-term morbidity and mortality rates in humans, rhythm control does not appear to have advantages over rate control; however, early abolishment of paroxysmal AF may have potential benefits including reduction of the extent of atrial fibrosis.16 Paroxysmal AF contributes to both structural and electrical remodeling of the atria, which may further worsen atrial dysfunction and increase the risk of thromboembolic complications.7–9 A rhythm control strategy was attempted in the dog of the present report because of the recent onset of AF; the short duration of AF may have increased the likelihood of successful cardioversion given that the time during which electrical remodeling could have occurred was considered to be relatively short.

Results from studies14,17,18 of dogs indicate that restoration of normal sinus rhythm can occur quickly following administration of class I antiarrhythmic drugs, such as lidocaine, for cases in which vagal tone is suspected to contribute to the maintenance of persistent AF. Lidocaine is most often used in the treatment of ventricular arrhythmias in dogs, and it is usually not considered for treatment of supraventricular arrhythmias such as AF.10 The mechanism by which lidocaine converts AF to sinus rhythm is unclear, but proposed theories include sodium channel blockade that causes a prolongation of the postrepolarization refractoriness, thereby resulting in increased reentrant wavelength; sodium channel blockade that increases the excitable gap of the reentrant wave; sodium channel blockade that decreases the generation of secondary wavelets; or direct blockade of cardiac muscarinic receptors, thereby causing opposition of parasympathetic stimulation.17 Lidocaine was chosen for treatment of the dog of the present report because it was considered likely that vagal tone had a role in the initiation and maintenance of AF. A relatively low lidocaine dosage was chosen to minimize adverse events, such as gastrointestinal tract disturbances, neurotoxicosis, or promotion of arrhythmia.19 Amiodarone alone or in combination with electrical cardioversion was considered a suitable alternative option had lidocaine treatment not successfully converted AF to sinus rhythm.

Deviation of the ST segment reflects heterogeneity of repolarization of the ventricular myocardium.3 ST-segment depression has been associated with intraventricular conduction delays, left ventricular hypertrophy, myocardial hypoxia, or digoxin toxicosis.3 ST-segment depression may be identified in dogs that have AF and a rapid ventricular response rate that is secondary to myocardial ischemia resulting from increased myocardial oxygen demand and decreased time for diastolic coronary arterial blood flow.20 For the case described in the present report, the ST-segment depression was noted prior to the onset of AF, most likely in association with left ventricular hypertrophy and the left bundle branch block.

For the dog of the present report, AF was converted to sinus tachycardia with administration of lidocaine, which suggested that enhanced vagal tone contributed to the initiation of AF. Additionally, the dog's enlarged heart increased the risk for recurrence of this abnormal rhythm; therefore, treatment with amiodarone was recommended to prevent arrhythmia recurrence.

articles.interpretacion_ecg: The 6-lead ECG recording (Figure 1) confirmed a variable heart rate ranging from 90 to 150 beats/min because of cyclic pauses. These pauses were characterized by R-R intervals of approximately twice the duration of the preceding R-R interval, consistent with sinoatrial block. The QRS complexes were narrow (60 milliseconds; reference range,1 < 70 milliseconds) with a physiologic electrical axis (+90°; reference range,1 +40° to +100°) and were always preceded by P waves of normal height (0.3 mV; reference range,1 < 0.4 mV) and duration (30 milliseconds; reference range,1 < 40 milliseconds). On the basis of these findings, the underlying rhythm was classified as sinus respiratory arrhythmia with probable sinoatrial block. However, changes in P-wave morphology were also occasionally observed (Figure 2), with abnormal P′ waves characterized by a notched (or bifid) negative morphology in lead II and prolonged duration (80 milliseconds), with or without a preceding pause. Such P-wave alterations lasted up to 30 seconds before disappearing and reappeared from time to time. These abnormal P′ waves were consistent with abnormal atrial conduction. Additionally, the presence of P′ waves was systematically associated with a P′R interval of 120 milliseconds versus 100 milliseconds for PR intervals.

articles.discusion:
Discussion

The dog described in the present report did not have any clinical signs except for the marked variation in heart rate, which was the reason for the cardiac consultation. This sinus arrhythmia was concomitant with both sinoatrial block and interatrial block (IAB) and was not associated with any echocardiographically apparent structural heart disease.

Blocks at the atrial level include IAB and other interatrial cardiac conduction disturbances such as atrial dissociation and atrial aberrancy.2–4 IAB is defined as a prolonged conduction time between the right and left atria due to an impulse delay or blockage, most often involving the Bachmann bundle.3 The Bachmann bundle is 1 of the 4 right-to-left atrial conduction pathways in the upper part of the atria.3,4 IAB typically results in prolonged P-wave duration on ECG tracings and represents a risk factor for supraventricular arrhythmias, including atrial fibrillation.3

In human patients, IAB is associated with various degrees of atrial structure abnormalities, including cellular destruction and increased intercellular collagen volume related to atrial fibrosis.5 It has been reported in the context of various ischemic, inflammatory, and infiltrative cardiac diseases as well as in the case of overstretch of the atrial walls and, more specifically, left atrial enlargement,3–8 with a significant correlation between P-wave duration and left atrial size.9 Lastly, IAB may also be related to degenerative processes, explaining why its prevalence significantly increases with age, with > 40% of humans > 50 years old being affected.3,10 Spontaneous IAB has been reported once in a Boxer and was associated with a heart base tumor occupying most of the left atrial cavity and leading to an enlarged left atrium.11 Additionally, IAB has been experimentally induced in dogs by producing discrete surgical lesions at the atrial level. These lesions affected P-wave morphology, polarity, and duration, depending on the site of the lesion and the pattern of atrial pacing.12

Similar to atrioventricular conduction blocks, IAB may be classified as first-, second-, or third-degree; corresponding to partial; intermittent; and advanced IAB, respectively.3,4,13 These IAB types can be accurately diagnosed with electroanatomic mapping techniques and also with several well-defined diagnostic criteria using surface ECG recordings.

Under physiologic conditions, the P wave in lead II recordings, but also lead I, III, and aVF recordings, is composed of an initial ascending slope representing right atrial activation and a descending slope corresponding to left atrial activation.2 First-degree IAB, also called partial IAB, is defined as an electric impulse conducted from the right to the left atrium through normal pathways, but with a delay in the Bachmann bundle area.2–4 It is typically characterized by an increased P-wave duration with a normal P-wave axis and usually a bimodal or notched morphology in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF). A similar P-wave aspect may be observed on surface ECG recordings in the case of left atrial enlargement without IAB (ie, a mitral P wave). Indeed, stretching of the atria increases the duration of atrial conduction, thus mimicking first-degree IAB.3

Third-degree IAB, also called advanced IAB, is defined by an electrical impulse completely blocked in the Bachmann bundle area, leading to abnormal caudocranial left atrial activation from the coronary sinus. It is typically characterized by an increased P-wave duration with various other identifiable aspects, including a positive-negative morphology in the inferior leads.3,4

Second-degree IAB is an intermittent phenomenon that can manifest with partial or advanced morphology patterns. Intermittency can be the result of changes in electrophysiologic characteristics induced by variations in cycle length in association with changes in heart rate, exactly as happens in bradycardia- or tachycardia-induced aberrant intraventricular conduction.4,13 In the present case, IAB was intermittent, lasting up to 30 seconds and reappearing from time to time, which is consistent with second-degree IAB. However, the P-wave morphology was notched negative (ie, negative-negative), which does not exactly correspond to typical P-wave morphologies with partial or advanced IAB. The most likely explanation for such a P-wave morphology is that the right atrium had undergone caudocranial activation as well as the left atrium. Most likely, the craniocaudal propagation of the impulse arising from the sinus node was cranially blocked toward the left and the right atrium, so that both atria were caudocranially activated. This hypothesis is supported by an experimental study in dogs12 that revealed a prolonged double-negative P-wave morphology following an induced lesion in the Bachmann bundle with the atria then paced from the posterior left atrium.

Interestingly, the ECG tracing of the dog reported here also revealed sinoatrial block, which is known to be a form of exit block from the sinus node. This latter could have affected the craniocaudal activation of the right atrium, thus providing this unique P′-wave morphology. The lack of apparent structural abnormality suggests that the most likely hypothesis would be a functional conduction block, of which the more likely cause is increased vagal tone.2 The dog showed second-degree IAB, sinoatrial block, and sinus arrhythmia, and it was assumed that all of these findings were the effects of a common cause (ie, parasympathetic surge).

In conclusion, to the authors’ knowledge, this is the first report detailing spontaneous second-degree IAB in a dog that was not associated with a structural abnormality but induced by a modulating factor (vagal surge).

articles.descripcion_del_caso:
A 15-year-old 30-kg (66-lb) spayed female Labrador Retriever was referred to the Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital at the University of California-Davis for evaluation of exercise intolerance and decreased appetite. The dog was not receiving any cardiac medications at the time of the referral evaluation. Five years prior to the evaluation, a diagnosis of myxomatous mitral valve degeneration had been made. At that time, echocardiography revealed that the dog had apparently normal left ventricular systolic function, mild mitral valve regurgitation, mild left atrial enlargement, and mild left ventricular eccentric hypertrophy with no evidence of right ventricular hypertrophy, and ECG revealed a normal sinus rhythm with right bundle branch block.

On physical examination, the dog was quiet, alert, and responsive. Its respiratory rate was 52 breaths/min, and rectal temperature was 37.9°C (100.3°F). The mucous membranes were pink, and the capillary refill time was 1.5 seconds. On cardiac auscultation, heart rhythm was irregularly irregular, and the heart rate was 240 to 260 beats/min. A grade 3/6 left apical systolic murmur was ausculted. Bilaterally weak femoral pulses with frequent pulse deficits were detected.

At the referral evaluation, initial diagnostic investigations included serum biochemical analyses and echocardiography. Abnormal serum biochemical findings included mild hypoproteinemia (5.2 g/dL; reference range, 5.4 to 7.6 g/dL) and mild azotemia (BUN concentration, 28 mg/dL [reference range, 5 to 21 mg/dL]; creatinine concentration, 1.3 mg/dL [reference range, 0.3 to 1.2 mg/dL]). Echocardiographically, moderate regurgitation through both atrioventricular (AV) valves, moderate left atrial dilation, moderate left ventricular eccentric hypertrophy, mild right atrial dilation, and mild right ventricular eccentric hypertrophy were detected. Electrocardiography was performed (Figure 1).
articles.interpretacion_ecg:
The 6-lead ECG evaluation revealed prolonged duration of the QRS complexes (80 milliseconds; reference range, up to 60 milliseconds in dogs); 2 forms of QRS complex morphologies were evident1 (Figure 1). Two potential origins for a wide QRS complex rhythm include either ventricular ectopy or supraventricular rhythm with bundle branch block. The predominant rhythm was tachycardic, with a mean ventricular response rate of 180 beats/min; QRS complexes that had the other detected morphology occurred intermittently, and these complexes were premature in relation to the underlying rate. Sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia generally involves the same cycle length, resulting in a constant coupling interval. Although monomorphic ventricular tachycardia can occasionally be associated with an irregular R-R interval, there is generally some periodicity to the irregularity (ie, regularly irregular heart rhythm). The irregularly irregular R-R interval prompted a diagnosis of supraventricular tachycardia with ventricular conduction disturbance, even though multifocal ventricular tachycardia was still a possibility. The absence of P waves, presence of fine undulations along the baseline, and the irregularly irregular R-R interval identified the supraventricular tachycardia as atrial fibrillation. The initial negative deflection of QRS complexes in lead II indicated conduction disturbance in the right bundle branch. Interestingly, the morphology of the QRS complexes at this time was identical to the QRS complex morphology recorded 5 years earlier when the dog was in normal sinus rhythm with right bundle branch block. The intermittent QRS complexes that had the other morphological form detected during the referral ECG examination were considered ventricular premature complexes of right ventricular origin.

To control the ventricular response rate of atrial fibrillation, treatment with antiarrhythmic medications was instituted; the dog was given digoxin (0.003 mg/kg [0.0014 mg/lb], PO, q 12 h), and a controlled-release formulation of diltiazem hydrochloride (3 mg/kg [1.4 mg/lb], PO, q 12 h). One week later, a recheck evaluation was performed to assess the clinical condition of the dog, serum digoxin concentration, and the effect of antiarrhythmic medications on cardiac rhythm and rate. Repeated ECG revealed much slower ventricular response rate (mean, 130 beats/min; Figure 2), which was considered evidence that successful rate control of the atrial fibrillation had been achieved through the negative dromotropic effect (slowing of AV nodal conduction) of the medications. Three characteristic features of atrial fibrillation were still observed: absence of P waves, fine undulations along the baseline, and irregularly irregular R-R intervals. No ventricular premature complexes were detected at this examination. The dog regained its normal appetite and had an improved energy level 2 to 3 days after starting cardiac medications. However, the dog's appetite decreased 3 days later. Serum digoxin concentration was evaluated and was mildly high (2.0 ng/mL; reference range, 0.5 to 1.5 ng/mL). After the dosage of digoxin was decreased by half, the dog's appetite returned to normal and heart rate remained well controlled.

articles.discusion:
Discussion

Cardiac structural disorders that increase atrial wall stress predispose affected hearts to atrial fibrillation, whereas atrial fibrillation may develop without any cardiac or systemic disease, a condition that is known as lone atrial fibrillation. Long-standing and rapid atrial fibrillation may lead to electrical remodeling in the atria (shortening of refractory period, slowing of conduction velocity, and alteration in expression of ion channels) and myocardial failure in the ventricles (eg, tachycardia-induced systolic dysfunction [socalled tachycardiomyopathy]), which result in lethargy, exercise intolerance, congestive heart failure, and ultimately cardiovascular-related death.2

Atrial fibrillation is characterized by multiple disorganized and microreentrant circuits in the atria. The mechanisms of spatiotemporal organization of electrical activity in the atria during atrial fibrillation are not conclusively understood. However, there is increasing experimental evidence that pulmonary veins or the ligament of Marshall is a crucial source of impulse initiation in atrial fibrillation in canine cardiac tissue preparations.3 A single dominant reentry circuit (mother rotor) originating from these areas is broken down into multiple waves in the atrial tissue, producing 400 to 600 randomly and irregularly propagating electrical impulses.4 Propagation of reentrant waves of atrial fibrillation to the ventricles primarily depends on the relative refractoriness of the AV node. Atrial depolarizations that are blocked in the AV node and are not conducted to the ventricle can cause slow conduction or block of a subsequent atrial impulse through the AV node. This phenomenon is known as concealed conduction within the node and is considered to have an essential role in causing a variable degree of penetration of the AV node and producing irregularly irregular ventricular coupling intervals in atrial fibrillation.5 Because atrial mechanical function is absent, there is no discernable P wave identified on the ECG tracings during atrial fibrillation; instead, fine or coarse undulations along the baseline are present.

Treatment for atrial fibrillation involves 1 of 2 therapeutic strategies: restoration of normal sinus rhythm (rhythm control) or slowing of the ventricular response rate (rate control). In humans with atrial fibrillation, morbidity and mortality rates are comparable regardless of therapeutic strategy undertaken.6 Rhythm control in humans can be accomplished via administration of antiarrhythmic agents (sodium channel blockers or potassium channel blockers), rapid atrial pacing, catheter ablation, or electrical cardioversion.7 Although cardioversion has been shown to be safe and effective in dogs, recurrence of atrial fibrillation is common, particularly in dogs with underlying structural heart disease.8 Rate control is primarily achieved via administration of antiarrhythmic agents that have negative dromotropic effects on the AV node, including β-adrenoceptor blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, or digoxin. Gelzer et al9 reported that treatment with a combination of digoxin and diltiazem resulted in better ventricular rate control and maintained a mean heart rate < 140 beats/min more consistently than did treatment with either drug alone in dogs with chronic atrial fibrillation. However, the clinical importance of this combination treatment, compared with the effects of monotherapy, was not addressed by those investigators and remains to be elucidated. Results of a recent clinical trial10 in humans indicated that less strict (lenient) rate control (ie, maintenance of resting heart rate < 110 beats/min) is not inferior to strict rate control (ie, maintenance of resting heart rate < 80 beats/min) with regard to prevention of cardiovascular morbidity and death attributed to cardiovascular causes in patients with chronic atrial fibrillation. A clinical trial in veterinary patients to determine an optimal target range of ventricular response rate that prevents development of clinical signs and heart failure and improves quality of life and long-term survival time is warranted. In the dog of this report, the combination of digoxin and diltiazem resulted in a notable reduction of ventricular response rate of atrial fibrillation and greatly improved the dog's clinical condition. In addition, a positive response to administration of antiarrhythmic medication and subsequent ECG findings confirmed the diagnosis of atrial fibrillation with right bundle branch block and ruled out the possibility of multifocal ventricular tachycardia. If ventricular tachycardia had been suspected initially, drug challenge with IV administration of diltiazem would have been highly useful to establish the definitive diagnosis immediately. In this dog, the cause of the atrial fibrillation was likely a result of electrical and pathological remodeling in the atria associated with progression of chronic myxomatous degeneration of the mitral and tricuspid valves.

Right or left bundle branch block develops as a result of underlying cardiac disease or rate-dependent aberrancy. There are 3 proposed mechanisms to explain rate-dependent aberrant ventricular conduction: stimulation during phase 3 of the action potential (tachycardia-dependent aberrancy), retrograde concealed conduction (manifested as ventricular arrhythmias), and stimulation during phase 4 of Purkinje fiber action potentials (bradycardia-dependent aberrancy).11 In particular, it is known that right bundle branch block is the more common form because the refractory period is longer in the right bundle branch than it is in the left bundle branch.12 The dog of this report had a history of right bundle branch block 5 years prior to the referral evaluation, and wide QRS complexes were repeatedly detected via ECG even after the mean heart rate was normalized. These observations suggested that the wide QRS complexes were associated with pathological changes in the right bundle branch and that they did not have an aberrancy-related cause.

articles.descripcion_del_caso: A 6-year-old 430-kg (946-lb) Standardbred gelding with a history of intermittent upper airway noise was examined following completion of a race as part of a track safety initiative. The horse had just paced a mile in 1 minute and 53 seconds and finished in third place (crossing the finishing line 1 second after the winner). After the race, the trainer noticed no abnormalities except that the horse required more time than usual for cooldown. During the scheduled physical examination, the horse had a rapid regular cardiac rhythm with a heart rate of 200 beats/min and visible pulses in the jugular veins. The horse was tachypneic and hyperthermic, consistent with recent exertion. Electrocardiography was performed by use of a handheld clipless digital recording device.a
articles.interpretacion_ecg:
An initial postrace ECG recording (Figure 1) was obtained with a handheld device that collects data from a single, nonstandard lead (similar to a base apex lead) when placed over the left heart base just behind the triceps brachii muscle. The first tracing revealed a sustained uniform tachyarrhythmia, with a rapid regular rhythm at a rate of 205 beats/min; uniform QRS complexes (QRS complex duration, 90 milliseconds), an elevated ST segment, and tall, positive T waves. P waves were not visible and were presumed to be buried within the other complexes.

Interpretation of the ECG findings was made in light of the horse's recent exertion. The heart rate was considered inappropriately high given that the recording was obtained 14 minutes after completion of the race when the heart rate would be expected to have decreased to < 120 beats/min. Interpretation of QRS complex width was difficult because of a lack of published information regarding the effects of exercise and heart rate on QRS complex duration in horses. A QRS complex duration of 90 milliseconds is considered normal for a horse at rest. The ST-segment elevation and tall T waves were considered typical for the high heart rate because similar changes are associated with sinus tachycardia at comparable heart rates.1

The inability to clearly identify p waves made differentiation between ventricular and supraventricular tachycardia difficult; however, a diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia was supported by the presence of jugular pulsations. Jugular pulsations are produced when there is dysynchrony of the atria and ventricles such as that which develops during ventricular tachycardia. The right atrium contracts against the closed tricuspid valve, causing blood to reflux from the atrium into the jugular veins, resulting in a visible jugular pulsation. With sustained atrial tachycardia, this dysynchrony does not occur and therefore jugular pulsations are not generated.

The horse was treated with lidocaine hydrochloride (0.5 mg/kg [0.23 mg/lb], IV) twice (injections were administered 15 minutes apart). Conversion to a normal sinus rhythm was evident 5 minutes after the second dose of lidocaine (approx 90 minutes after completion of the race; Figure 2). At this time, the QRS complex polarity was considered normal for the applied lead system. Following conversion, the horse visibly relaxed and the jugular pulses were no longer visible.

Approximately 90 minutes after completion of the race, a blood sample was collected to obtain plasma for venous blood gas analysis and assessment of electrolyte (sodium, potassium, chloride, and calcium) and cardiac troponin I (cTnI) concentrations. Venous blood gas results and plasma electrolyte concentrations were within reference limits, but plasma cTnI concentration was high (0.38 ng/mL; reference range, ≤ 0.07 ng/mLb). The horse was rehydrated PO. Dexamethasone (0.08 mg/kg [0.04 mg/lb]) and flunixin meglumine (1.1 mg/kg [0.5 mg/lb]) were administered IV, and electrolyte paste was administered PO. A Holter monitorc was placed to obtain a 24-hour recording, and the horse was referred for monitoring and further investigation of the cause of the tachyarrhythmia.

On arrival at the referral hospital, cardiac auscultation revealed that the cardiac rhythm was regular and heart rate was within reference limits. A grade 2/6 holosystolic, blowing, band-shaped murmur with the point of maximal intensity over the tricuspid valve and a grade 1/6 holosystolic, blowing, band-shaped murmur over the mitral valve were detected. Electrocardiographic evaluation revealed a normal sinus rhythm. On the basis of 2-D, M-mode, and Doppler echocardiographic findings, heart size and myocardial function were considered normal and there were no structural abnormalities of the myocardium. Mild tricuspid and mitral valve regurgitation were evident. The 24-hour Holter monitor recording revealed 2 ventricular premature complexes of differing morphologies and 35 uniform supraventricular premature depolarizations. Results of a CBC and assessment of plasma fibrinogen concentration were within reference limits. Serum biochemical analysis revealed mildly high concentrations of creatinine (1.9 mg/dL; reference range, 0.6 to 1.8 mg/dL) and total protein (7.0 g/dL; reference range, 4.6 to 6.9 g/dL) consistent with mild dehydration. The horse was discharged from the hospital after 2 days; the treatment plan included administration of dexamethasone (tapering dosage), stall rest, and paddock turnout with no forced exercise for 3 weeks. A follow-up, 24-hour continuous ECG performed at the end of the 3-week period revealed 4 supraventricular premature depolarizations but no evidence of ventricular ectopy. It was recommended that the horse undergo an ECG assessment during exercise and a dynamic upper airway evaluation before returning to racing. Unfortunately, those procedures were not performed and the horse was returned to racing, subsequently claimed, and lost to follow-up.

articles.discusion:
Discussion

Arrhythmias in horses that are associated with racing have been occasionally reported in the veterinary medical literature,2–4 with atrial fibrillation being the most common. Diagnosis of a tachyarrhythmia in the race recovery period is typically contingent upon the horse developing clinical signs or having a sufficiently poor performance to warrant physical examination. The clinical signs of ventricular tachycardia in horses may include sweating, agitation, colic-like behavior, tachypnea, and jugular pulsations.5,6 The effects on racing performance may be none, mild, or dramatic depending on the point at which the arrhythmia develops during the race. In the horse of this report, the diagnosis was made on the basis of the ECG findings; the horse's ECG evaluation was prompted by the track's cardiac safety initiative and not by any specific performance problems or physical examination abnormalities. Although the horse's trainer had noticed that it took more time than usual for cooldown, signs of mild anxiety and jugular pulsations were only noted retrospectively after abnormalities in the initial ECG recording were detected. The signs of anxiety were made more evident when the horse visibly relaxed after converting back to a normal sinus rhythm. Tachypnea and sweating are expected postrace findings in horses and did not aid in the identification of a tachyarrhythmia in this case setting. Given the performance of the horse of this report, it is likely that the arrhythmia developed either very near the end of the race or in the race recovery period. In a recent report7 of arrhythmias in Standardbred racehorses, complex ventricular arrhythmias that occurred in the race recovery period were detected in 55 of 345 race starts. Those arrhythmias resolved quickly and spontaneously and would have likely remained undetected had telemetric monitoring not been in place.

During exercise, there are substantial autonomic and homeostatic changes that could contribute to the development of cardiac arrhythmias. These include autonomic tone changes, marked disturbances in plasma potassium concentration, and alterations in acid-base balance. In physiologically normal mammals, these changes are proposed to occur in a balanced manner, each affording some protection from the proarrhythmic effects of the other.8 In the postexercise period, this balance of factors may be more difficult to maintain because rapid alterations in autonomic tone occur with rebound parasympathetic activity and decreasing sympathetic tone. Although these are normal physiologic mechanisms responsible for cardiovascular recovery, they represent a period of autonomic instability that may be further influenced by sympathetic hyperactivity due to stress or excitement or by a reduced rate of parasympathetic reactivation.7 When combined with other homeostatic disturbances or myocardial abnormalities, ventricular arrhythmias may develop.

Other predisposing factors for ventricular tachycardia include primary myocardial disease or inflammation, hypoxic myocardial injury, myocardial toxins, electrolyte abnormalities, and acid-base or other metabolic disturbances.5,9,10 Potassium is the electrolyte that receives the most attention as a possible mediator of cardiac arrhythmias because both hyperkalemia and hypokalemia can affect action potentials in cardiac tissue. Hypokalemia increases the resting membrane potential, action potential duration, and refractory period of cardiac tissue, leading to increased automaticity and conduction disturbances.11 Profuse sweating and the use of furosemide in the treatment of exercise-induced pulmonary hemorrhage may predispose racehorses to development of hypokalemia and arrhythmias. Hypokalemia increases the risk for ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death in humans.12 In contrast to hypokalemia, hyperkalemia decreases the resting membrane potential, action potential duration, and effective refractory period of cardiac tissue, which can also lead to increased automaticity and conduction disturbances. During high-intensity exercise, hyperkalemia develops secondary to release of potassium from skeletal muscle.13 In horses, plasma potassium concentration returns to baseline value usually within 5 to 10 minutes after completing exercise.14 After exercise in some human athletes, circulating potassium concentrations may decrease from pre-exercise values and remain low for up to 90 minutes.13 Plasma potassium concentration prior to exercise was not measured in the horse of this report; however, plasma potassium concentration was within reference limits approximately 90 minutes after exercise. Clinically important alterations of the circulating potassium concentration during and immediately after exercise could not be ruled out. The horse's high plasma cTnI concentration may have been an indication of preexisting myocardial inflammation or injury, hypoxic myocardial injury secondary to an upper airway disorder or lower airway inflammation, or poor myocardial perfusion secondary to the sustained tachyarrhythmia. Echocardiographic evaluation did not provide evidence of structural myocardial abnormalities, although small structural abnormalities may have easily been overlooked.

For the horse of this report, antiarrhythmic treatment consisted of IV administration of lidocaine prior to transportation to a referral facility. Delayed treatment of hemodynamically important ventricular arrhythmias (multiform arrhythmias or those with heart rates > 120 beats/min or R-on-T phenomena) is not recommended because affected horses are at risk for sudden death. Lidocaine (without epinephrine) is readily available and easily administered and should be on hand for veterinarians that deliver emergency medical care in racetrack or ambulatory settings. Lidocaine has a narrow therapeutic range in horses; consequently, it is usually administered in small boluses (0.5 mg/kg, IV, q 10 min up to total dose of 1.5 mg/kg [0.7 mg/lb]). Neurologic adverse effects including excitement and seizures may develop with higher dosages.15

Ventricular arrhythmias are of particular concern in racehorses because there is considerable danger to the rider or driver as well as other competitors on the track if a horse collapses or dies suddenly. Public perception of the sport may be adversely affected by such an event. Guidelines for human athletes with ventricular arrhythmias indicate that athletic activity should be delayed until a complete cardiac evaluation including echocardiographic evaluation and ECG assessments at rest, during exercise, and for a 24-hour period can be performed.16 For the horse of this report, ECG monitoring, upper airway evaluation, and blood gas and electrolyte analysis during exercise and collection and analysis of a postexercise bronchoalveolar lavage sample were indicated to identify potential predisposing factors for ventricular tachycardia and determine a prognosis for its safe return to racing.

articles.descripcion_del_caso: A 14-year-old spayed female mixed-breed dog was referred to the Clinica Veterinaria Malpensa because of frequent episodes of syncope (frequency, 1 to 5 episodes/d). At the initial evaluation, the dog appeared mildly depressed. The femoral pulse was bradyarrhythmic with a mean heart rate of 40 beats/min. Results of auscultation of the heart and lungs were considered normal, and no other clinical abnormalities were detected. Thoracic radiographic and echocardiographic findings were also considered normal. Twelve-lead surface ECG (6 peripheral standard leads and 6 precordial leads as previously described1; Figure 1) was performed with the dog placed in right lateral recumbency.
articles.interpretacion_ecg:
The 12-lead surface ECG tracing (Figure 1) revealed a severe bradyarrhythmia with a mean ventricular rate of 40 beats/min. The P-wave duration was 40 milliseconds (reference range, < 40 milliseconds) and amplitude was 0.4 mV (reference range, < 0.4 mV), with a sinus rate of 140 beats/min and a normal P-wave axis on the frontal plane (+80°; reference range, −18° to +90°). An atrioventricular (AV) conduction disturbance with lack of concordance between atrial and ventricular depolarization rate was evident. Only a few P waves were followed by ventricular QRS complexes with an AV conduction ratio of 2:1 (ie, 2 P waves [1 unconducted and 1 conducted] for 1 QRS complex) that sometimes evolved into advanced (or complete) AV block (AV conduction ratios of 3:1 and 4:1). The PQ interval for the conducted beats was 120 milliseconds (reference range, 60 to 130 milliseconds).

These features were consistent with a second-degree (2:1 type) AV block with episodes of advanced AV block. Moreover, intraventricular conduction disturbance was evident because of a prolongation of the QRS complexes (duration, 80 milliseconds; reference range, < 70 milliseconds) and tall, slurred, and delayed R waves in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF) and left precordial lead tracings. The rate-corrected QT interval (QTc) was slightly prolonged (duration, 249 milliseconds; reference range, 150 to 240 milliseconds). The mean electrical axis of the QRS complex was +82°, which was within reference limits (+40° to +100°); there was positive polarity of QRS complexes in the inferior lead tracings and negative polarity of QRS complexes in the V1 precordial lead tracing. Moreover, the V1 precordial lead tracing revealed an rS-type configuration of the QRS complexes. All of these findings were consistent with a complete left bundle branch block (LBBB). The QRS complexes of the conducted beats had normal Q waves in the inferior lead tracings. The presence of Q waves in the lead I tracing may have indicated normal early depolarization of the interventricular septum because the block of conduction occurred in the distal ramifications of the left bundle branch. This type of LBBB, called postdivisional block, is typically characterized by a marked prolongation of the QRS complex duration (> 80 milliseconds). On the other hand, the absence of Q waves in the lead I tracing suggests an abnormal direction of the first vector of depolarization of the ventricular mass caused by a proximal LBBB (troncular block or divisional block). In dogs, Q waves are sometimes evident in lead I even in the presence of a troncular LBBB, and this early depolarization force derives from the right ventricular lateral wall.2

Because of the concomitant presence of LBBB and an AV conduction disturbance, a trifascicular block was suspected. Given that the ventricular conduction system is composed anatomically of a right bundle branch and a left bundle branch (which is formed by 2 fascicles, the left anterior fascicle and the left posterior fascicle), a concomitant or intermittent interruption of all 3 branches is defined as trifascicular block.

Permanent endocavitary pacemaker implantation is indicated in dogs that are clinically affected by high-degree AV block because of the high risk of developing complete AV block. In the dog of this report, a VVI (single-chamber, ventricular-sensing, ventricular-pacing [in the inhibited mode]) pacemaker was implanted by introducing the single electrostimulator catheter through the right jugular vein and fixing its end on the right ventricular apex; the pacemaker was then positioned in a subcutaneous pocket on the dog's neck. A ventricular stimulation rate of 60 beats/min was set with a hysteresis of 40 beats/min to promote spontaneous rhythm with normal AV conduction. VVI-type pacemakers operate both stimulating and sensing only at the ventricular level and at a planned activation rate. No atrial sensing is performed with this type of pacemaker used in this manner, and ventricular depolarization occurs slowly through myocardial cells, producing wide QRS complexes.

Electrocardiography was performed after pacemaker implantation (Figure 2). In the tracings, an alternation between paced and spontaneous beats occurred. The paced beats had a low amplitude spike followed by wide QRS complexes with negative voltage in the inferior lead tracings and positive voltage in left precordial lead tracings. The spontaneous beats had a bifascicular block configuration with an LBBB morphology of the QRS complexes. In the tracings, a pause of 1,500 milliseconds was recorded after a second spontaneous beat, which induced reactivation of the pacemaker. Some nonconducted P waves were evident in all of the ECG lead tracings.

After a few days, the dog was discharged from the hospital. During a 2-year follow-up period, no other syncopal events were reported by the owners and no pacemaker abnormalities were recorded during serial ECG examinations.
